segmenti.tekst: [Arabic recitation]

So, this is a hadith circle (halaqah). The hadith of the Messenger of Allah, sallallahu alayhi wa sallam (peace be upon him), is revelation, dear brothers and esteemed sisters. And just as the Qur'anic text leaves a special impression and a special effect on the one who reads it, who listens to it, who understands it, so too the hadiths of the Messenger of Allah, Muhammad, sallallahu alayhi wa sallam, as we read them, listen to them, comment on them [unclear], leave an impression, and we see from the text itself that it is revelation from Allah the Exalted, jalla sha'nuhu.

And that is why the Islamic scholars say that those scholars who kept company most with the hadiths of the Messenger of Allah, Muhammad, alayhis-salatu was-salam, were the happiest, in the sense that they sent the most blessings (salawat) upon the Prophet Muhammad, alayhis-salatu was-salam.

So whenever a hadith and the Prophet Muhammad, alayhis-salam, are mentioned, one should send blessings and peace upon him, and simply, from these circles and gatherings people will come out rich and successful.

I have called this lecture "Travelling in Pursuit of Knowledge", and in other words we can also call this lecture "The Wisest and Most Intelligent Delegation That Came to the Prophet Muhammad, sallallahu alayhi wa sallam".

What is it about? Ibn Abbas, radiyallahu ta'ala anhu (may Allah be pleased with him), narrates, and Bukhari and Muslim record, that the delegation of Abd al-Qays came to the Prophet Muhammad, sallallahu alayhi wa sallam.

That was in the ninth year after the Hijra. So, among the first delegations that came to the Prophet Muhammad, sallallahu alayhi wa sallam, was this delegation of Abd al-Qays. And the Messenger of Allah, alayhis-salatu was-salam, asks them: "Manil-wafd?" – who is the delegation, who are you?

They said: "We are Rabi'ah, we are from the tribe of Rabi'ah." And then the Prophet Muhammad, sallallahu alayhi wa sallam – they had come to the Prophet in Madinah – says to them: "Marhaban bil-wafdi ghayra khazaya wa la nadama" – he says: "Welcome, O delegation, which is neither humiliated nor will have regrets."

Then they say to the Prophet, sallallahu alayhi wa sallam – after the Prophet, sallallahu alayhi wa sallam, had welcomed them – then they say: "Ya Rasulallah, O Messenger of Allah, we come to you from a distant place."

That is the region which today in Saudi Arabia is called Al-Ahsa, that is, the area over there beyond Riyadh, towards Bahrain. It was from that area that they came to the Messenger of Allah, sallallahu alayhi wa sallam.

And they say: "We cannot come to you all the time, because between us and you there is an unbelieving people from the tribe of Mudar. And the only time we have the opportunity to come to you is during the sacred months."

Why? Because during the sacred months the Arabs did not wage war. They would not fight even with their fiercest enemies. Even their executioners and the killers of their closest ones – fathers, brothers, relatives – the Arabs would not trouble in any way.

A sacred month – in those sacred months they would not wage war, they would not shed blood. They say: "We can only come in the sacred months, because we then pass through enemy territory when safety is guaranteed. And therefore, O Messenger of Allah,

command us something that we will convey to those who are among our people" – meaning, we are the representatives of a great people – "and on the basis of which we will enter Jannah (Paradise)", subhanallah. It says: after that they asked him about drink, and they asked him about certain kinds of drink.

And the Prophet, sallallahu alayhi wa sallam, in reply commanded them four things and forbade them four things. The Prophet, sallallahu alayhi wa sallam, said at the very beginning: "I command you iman, I command you iman and belief."

And then after that he says to them: "Do you know what iman is and what belief is?" And they say: "Allah and His Messenger know best." And then the Messenger of Allah, sallallahu alayhi wa sallam, says to them – pay attention to the answer, brothers, to how the Prophet answers them – he says: "Belief, or iman, is that you testify that Allah, jalla sha'nuhu, is the only true deity who deserves to be worshipped, and that Muhammad, sallallahu alayhi wa sallam, is the Messenger of Allah, that you perform the prayer, that you give zakat, that you fast the month of Ramadan, and also that you set aside one fifth of your spoils of war."

And he forbade them four kinds of vessels, which are made either from gourds, or from palm roots, or in some other way from wood, and then coated with pitch and the like. And he says: "Remember this well and inform the people who have remained behind you."

That is this story, the dialogue between the Messenger of Allah, sallallahu alayhi wa sallam, and this delegation. This hadith, my dear brothers and respected attendees, is one of the basic and fundamental hadiths when it comes to speaking about iman and belief.

The Islamic scholars who wrote books on belief, on aqidah, all included this hadith of the Messenger of Allah, Muhammad, sallallahu alayhi wa sallam. This is a well-known hadith, authentic, and it is found, besides the hadith collections of Bukhari and Muslim, in other hadith collections as well that were written gathering the hadiths of the Prophet Muhammad, Muhammad, sallallahu alayhi wa sallam.

Why did we say that this is the wisest delegation and the most intelligent delegation? Because this is among the first delegations that came to the Prophet Muhammad, sallallahu alayhi wa sallam. Afterwards the representatives of all the Arab tribes and all the peoples after them came to the Messenger of Allah, sallallahu alayhi wa sallam, gave their pledge, expressed their faith and so on, but they were the first.
And look how clever, how intelligent these representatives were. Some say there were 14 of them, some say there were 40, [unclear], but in any case these were chosen men.

Because chosen men are sent in a delegation. Not the whole people, or all the people, is sent; rather, those are chosen who are the most intelligent, the most perceptive, the most trustworthy, the most well-mannered. So, people are selected and then sent somewhere to carry out some task.

And this team of men covered, covered such a distance in order to ask the Messenger of Allah, Muhammad, sallallahu alayhi wa sallam, the most important question. So, they invested effort. That is almost, nearly a thousand kilometres.

If we were to measure that route which they travelled on camels – some were on foot, and some were on camels – over sand, under the sun, through all those unpleasant weather conditions in the desert, they came to talk with the Messenger of Allah, Muhammad, sallallahu alayhi wa sallam.

The leader of this delegation was al-Mundhir ibn A'idh, al-Ashajj of Abd al-Qays, so they say. He was at the head of this delegation. It is interesting: he was, of course, since he was at the head of the delegation, the most intelligent, the wisest, the sharpest.

When this delegation came to the Prophet, sallallahu alayhi wa sallam, in Madinah, when they arrived, when they saw Madinah, when they saw the mosque of the Messenger of Allah, Muhammad, sallallahu alayhi wa sallam, knowing that the Messenger of Allah was there, they scattered and ran, racing one another to see who would be the first to kiss the Prophet, who would be the first to [unclear] the Messenger of Allah, who would be the first to kiss his hand, alayhis-salatu was-salam.

Because imagine: today, when we go to Madinah, the Messenger of Allah, sallallahu alayhi wa sallam… we rejoice. We rejoice at his mosque. We know that the Messenger of Allah, sallallahu alayhi wa sallam, is there; it is the city of the Prophet, sallallahu alayhi wa sallam. Whoever enters Madinah is overcome by a special blessing (barakah), a special tranquillity and a special mercy.

Because the Messenger of Allah, sallallahu alayhi wa sallam, named Madinah Taybah – comfortable, pleasant, agreeable – and it truly is so, so. Imagine that you had the opportunity to visit Madinah while the Messenger of Allah, sallallahu alayhi wa sallam, was in it, to see the Prophet, sallallahu alayhi wa sallam – that is a great [unclear] for the believers.

And that is why these companions [unclear]. They scattered and ran to meet the Messenger of Allah, sallallahu alayhi wa sallam, as soon as possible. But al-Mundhir ibn A'idh, or al-Ashajj of Abd al-Qays, who was at the head of the column, he stayed [unclear].

He changed his clothes nicely – in some narrations it is stated that he even freshened up, bathed – he put on his most beautiful garment, put on perfume. Because, mind you, after such a long journey a person is in an unpleasant state and perhaps sweat and dirt and dust and so on can be noticed, but he removed all of that, and only then did he come to the Prophet, sallallahu alayhi wa sallam.

And when the Prophet saw him, he said: "Inna fika lakhaslatayni yuhibbuhumallahu wa rasuluh" – he said to him: "You are a man who has two qualities, two traits that Allah the Exalted and His Messenger love."
What are they? "Al-hilmu wal-anah." Al-hilm – gentleness, and al-anah – composure. Some Islamic scholars comment on this term, al-hilm, that is, they say that it is al-'aql, that it is reason.

So: you are intelligent and you are composed. You are gentle, you are intelligent and you are composed. And truly hastiness, hastiness – a person rushing ahead in expressing some position, in expressing some judgement, in anything – rushing ahead and hurrying can be fatal, with fatal consequences.
But people who are intelligent and who are wise do not rush ahead. They are collected, they are steady, they wait, they look at the situation from all angles, and only then do they react.

So, they think, they reflect, and then they speak, or, well, they act. They do not rush ahead, they do not say the first thing that comes to mind, and then regret it if it turns out to be a wrong position, a wrong, well, statement. And that is why it is very important for a Muslim to be steady both when he walks and when he speaks, and when he deals with people, and when he does something – to be stable, intelligent and steady.

And to keep company with such people. It is very important for a person to keep company with intelligent and clever people. Because just as a fruit tree can be grafted, so that from some wild fruit tree that is not of such good quality a good-quality, cultivated fruit tree is made, intelligence too can be grafted.
If a person keeps company with intelligent, clever, learned people, wise people, he takes on their qualities and their traits. Look, this is a dialogue between people who are the elite,

the first row (saff). Look at what kind of dialogue takes place between the Prophet Muhammad, sallallahu alayhi wa sallam, and these companions, the first, that is, Muslims. They do not talk much, but when they talk, or when they say something, when they speak – first of all, the question is very concise, very intelligent, succinct – and then the answer they receive from the Prophet Muhammad, sallallahu alayhi wa sallam, is even more beautiful, of even higher quality, with good manners (adab), with regard, with respect.

That is where, that is where the point is, my dear brothers. The point is that a person be a person of character, wise, of quality, that he adorn himself with the most distinguished virtues, the most beautiful traits – that is the point.
And the point is not that a person talks and converses any old way and says just anything, and that this simply causes later some behaviour that can have negative consequences.

This is also a lesson that at the head of a people, at the head of a community, at the head of a group and of a congregation there should be those who are most distinguished in knowledge, in reason, in wisdom, in composure, etc.

Because this delegation, and this people, the tribe of Rabi'ah, sent the most select men, and among them they appointed the most intelligent as amir and leader. Then the Prophet, sallallahu alayhi wa sallam – look at his good manners (adab) –

first asks them: "Manil-wafd?" – who are you? This is a basic, elementary question. It is established that when getting acquainted, when meeting, when inviting, when addressing someone, before any communication, the first and basic rule is to introduce oneself:

either to introduce yourself, or to ask the other side to introduce itself, so that you know how to deal properly and appropriately with the side you are coming into contact with, and the like. That is very important, my dear brothers. The Prophet, sallallahu alayhi wa sallam, says: "Who are you?"

And they, of course, say: "Rabi'ah, we are the tribe of Rabi'ah." Here there is also proof that a person may, for a small number of people or representatives, say "Rabi'ah", that is, introduce himself in the name of the whole people,

and mention the name of the whole, the whole, well, the whole people. Who are you? For example: "We are Muslims." That does not mean that all the Muslims of this world are there, no, but that group – they are Muslims, they are representatives, then, of the whole ummah. Or: "We are Bosniaks," and so on, and so forth. And then comes the most beautiful welcome from the best of hosts, from the Prophet.
The Prophet, sallallahu alayhi wa sallam, says: "Marhaba" – this is an Arabic word, dear brothers – which many Muslim peoples learned and adopted, among them us too, here, in the Balkans, in Sandžak.

We use the word "merhaba", and the Turks also use this word. It is an Arabic word. And the word "marhaba" comes from the word "rihab", which means spaciousness. And when you say, for example, to your guest, or to a traveller (musafir), when he comes to you, and you say "merhaba" to him, you are then saying to him: may my house be spacious, pleasant, comfortable for you; feel at ease.

All of that is what you mean when you say "merhaba" to him. That is why it is said: "rihabul-jannah" – in the expanses of Jannah. So the word "marhaba" is a fine custom of the Arabs, which we non-Arabs also use, and we should preserve that word as our heritage. It is very concise, very rich in meaning.
The Prophet says to them: "Welcome, O delegation, which is neither humiliated nor will have regrets, nor has regrets." Why is it not humiliated?

Here the Prophet praised them. And why do they have no regrets? This delegation accepted Islam without any fighting. Without any effort they came to the Messenger of Allah, sallallahu alayhi wa sallam, of their own accord. They came to him as Muslims.

Because, mind you, they address the Prophet: "Ya Rasulallah, O Messenger of Allah." Then they say: "Between us and you, O Messenger of Allah, is an unbelieving people," which means that they had already come as Muslims. And whoever accepts the truth and whoever accepts Islam in this way, on the basis of these most beautiful methods, without any special effort invested by the Muslim community, they are at a special, a special rank (darajah).

Because the Messenger of Allah, sallallahu alayhi wa sallam, conquered some territories by fighting, in order to free them from various tyrants (taghut) and dictators who were preventing people from listening to the truth, while this group came to the Messenger of Allah, sallallahu alayhi wa sallam, by themselves.

And the Prophet praised them: you will not regret, nor will you be, well, humiliated. And here too there is a message that the path of Islam, the path of truth, the path of the Qur'an and the path of the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah, sallallahu alayhi wa sallam, protects the individual, protects the family and protects the whole community from every form of humiliation and regret.

Whoever follows the right path will not be humiliated and will not regret, especially not in the Hereafter (akhirah). He will not, because, well, honour belongs to Allah, to the Messenger and to the believers.

Honour belongs to the believers, but the hypocrites are the ones who do not know it. Next, why did we call this lesson "Travelling in Pursuit of Knowledge"? They covered great distances to come to the Prophet, sallallahu alayhi wa sallam, to the best teacher, and to learn what is most beneficial and most valuable.

In Islamic culture and in the culture of this ummah, this custom and this practice – travelling in pursuit of knowledge – was established very long ago. Al-Khatib al-Baghdadi mentions in his books that the first to travel in pursuit of knowledge was Musa, alayhis-salatu was-salam.

Musa, as a prophet of Allah, to whom Jibril comes and brings revelation from Allah, jalla sha'nuhu, and knowledge from Allah, the Lord of all the worlds, travels and seeks someone more learned than himself – that was al-Khidr. Al-Khidr was more learned than him in some areas. And it was neither distasteful nor a humiliation for him to sit before al-Khidr and learn from him like a little child, like a student.
Respected attendees, for the sake of knowledge one should sacrifice what is most valuable: time, and wealth, and effort, and toil. Everything should be invested in pursuit of knowledge.

When we speak of knowledge, we mean all kinds of knowledge, all kinds of knowledge. For knowledge is divided into Sharia knowledge, knowledge of the religion – that is fard, an obligation on every Muslim, to learn the religion as much as he needs in order to [unclear] worship Allah.

And then it is an obligation for a certain group and certain individuals to specialise in the Sharia sciences. But these other fields and other sciences too – both natural and social, and every beneficial field and science – Muslims must have experts, the best experts.

The best experts. If the Muslims do not have the best experts in all these fields, they are all sinful before Allah, subhanahu wa ta'ala. They are all sinful before Allah, subhanahu wa ta'ala. Because knowledge is honour, knowledge is freedom, knowledge is power, but knowledge is also responsibility.

Knowledge is also responsibility. When Muslims have knowledge, they are a mercy to the worlds, a mercy to peoples, a mercy to states, a mercy to societies and so on, to all societies, to all of mankind. But when knowledge is possessed far from ethics and from fear of the Exalted Lord of all the worlds, then you have oppression (zulm), then you have dictatorships, then you have the humiliation of people, then you have the killing of people, and so on, and so forth.

So, my dear brothers, it is haram for Muslims to be illiterate. It is haram for Muslims to be illiterate. Muslim youth must be the most learned – I keep repeating that. But we base our knowledge on ethics, on morality and on fear of Allah the Exalted, subhanahu wa ta'ala.

The more we know, the humbler we become, the more submissive we become, because, as the Islamic scholars say: "al-'ilmu al-khashyah" – knowledge is humble awe. The one who has a spiritual foundation and then acquires knowledge – the more he knows, the humbler he is, the more submissive he is, the more approachable he is.

As opposed to the one who does not have that foundation, who does not have a spiritual and ethical foundation – the more knowledge he has, the more arrogant he is, the more puffed up he is, the more he humiliates people, he [unclear], and so on. And for a Muslim this is simply understood.

Whoever draws nourishment in the mosque easily understands that knowledge is from Allah the Exalted [unclear]. However much you know, [unclear]… As al-Khidr said to Musa: "O Musa, your knowledge and my knowledge compared to Allah's knowledge is like when a bird takes some sea water with its beak."
How much has it reduced that water? Well, that much – well, in the same way, our knowledge is nothing compared to Allah's knowledge. Next…

It is very important for a person to have the opportunity to study in his own place and in his own town, but also to travel in pursuit of knowledge – why not? Now Allah, jalla sha'nuhu, has made seeking knowledge so easy. There are so many methods, modern methods, distance learning, to acquire knowledge, to educate yourself. But the more of these conveniences we have, the stronger laziness becomes and the weaker ambitions become.

We must not be of weak ambition, and we must not allow laziness to attack us and overwhelm us and overpower us, and simply to live merely for some of our biological needs, far from these sublime spiritual, ethical and scholarly values.

Next: guidance is in the hands of Allah, guidance is in the hands of Allah. Look: the Messenger of Allah, sallallahu alayhi wa sallam, then the tribes of Mudar – and those are the tribes from which the Prophet, sallallahu alayhi wa sallam, descends – and then Rabi'ah.

That tribe was closer to the Messenger of Allah, sallallahu alayhi wa sallam, closer to the city of Madinah, closer to the revelation, closer to the truth, closer to the healthiest environment, the healthiest environment, but Allah guided these who were far away.

What does that mean? It means that guidance is in His hands. He is the One who gives guidance to whomever He wills. But here, very often, when I say this – guidance is in the hands of Allah, Allah guides whomever He wills, leaves in error whomever He wills – somehow, [unclear] our, our imagination… [unclear]: "Well, all right,
is that just?" Allah gives guidance to the one who deserves it. This is a very important matter. And whoever shows interest in it, whoever shows interest in guidance, Allah will give him guidance.

Whoever asks, whoever seeks, whoever prays, whoever wants it – Allah will give it to him… But whoever refuses, whoever turns his head away, whoever does not want it, whoever will not listen to the arguments and proofs, that is the category that will remain in error. Allah says: since they turned away from the right path, Allah made their hearts turn away from the right… And look at the mercy of Allah, subhanahu wa ta'ala, towards this people, Rabi'ah: across a great obstacle of an unbelieving, hostile, inimical people Allah guided them

to believe in the Prophet and to come under him. Then, that sacrifice in the way of Allah – one of the messages is: it is necessary to make a sacrifice in the way of Allah. Of course this is the greatest pleasure and sweetness, but a sacrifice is needed in the way of Allah: to set out, to show Allah that you want it, to get tired, to sweat. In every job, in every field, if you want to be an expert and a special specialist, you must sweat, days and nights must pass

of toil and effort, and then Allah, subhanahu wa ta'ala, opens things up for you and gives you real results. It is said in a line of verse: knowledge cannot be attained while your body is always rested and you never get tired.

It cannot. You must get tired, you must invest a little effort. In order for them to have this privilege – that we today here, 1400 years after this event, talk about this delegation, praise them, send blessings upon them and direct supplications to Allah for them – they had to… Because of the sincerity of their hearts and of the intentions in their hearts, in fact, Allah, subhanahu wa ta'ala, granted them acceptance (qabul), so that generations praise them until the Day of Judgement. My dear brothers, respected youth, O you who follow Muhammad, sallallahu alayhi wa sallam,

the best of men, O you and O we who worship the Lord of all the worlds, the Perfect and the Exalted, we must burn ourselves out in the way of Allah, subhanahu wa ta'ala. Do not spare energy, do not spare effort, do not spare toil in the way of Allah, subhanahu wa ta'ala.

Become the best in what you are, in where you are and in what you do, and become a role model, then, for all of mankind. And it is truly unacceptable that an ummah which is destined to lead and which has all [unclear] to lead should experience a state in which it is led by others, who worship all sorts of phenomena, appearances, images, frescoes, made-up stories.

An ummah that has the Qur'an and the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah, sallallahu alayhi wa sallam… But it is up to us – we can blame ourselves, and we only have the right to blame ourselves. It is not down to Allah, subhanahu wa ta'ala; Allah, jalla sha'nuhu, has given us the means and the opportunities.

Next, this too is a very important matter: that the Arabs were a people of strong character, a people of very strong character. Before Islam, yes, even before Islam character was at a high level among them. And character is very important, my dear brothers.

Without firm character, without a sound foundation in a person, he cannot be a good believer, nor a good scientist, nor a teacher, nor a leader, nor a son, nor a father, nor a brother, nor a friend, nor a businessman – he cannot be good at anything.
There must be character; the foundation is character. Mind you: these people are at war, that is, at war with one another, but when the sacred months come – that's it.

He sees his brother, that is, he sees his brother's killer by the Ka'bah – he does not trouble him. He would deal with him somewhere else, but there, on sacred territory, on sacred ground – no. Only a people of character can do that. That is why Allah, subhanahu wa ta'ala, sent them the first revelation and from them made and raised that finest, finest generation.

That is why it is very important, very significant, dear youth, dear believers, fathers, parents, brothers, sisters, to nurture and develop character in yourselves and in your children and in your youth. That is very important. Because today everything is being done in this modern world, where globalisation reigns, to tear down these foundations in man, in the individual, and in the community, and in the family:

so that there are no limits, no principles, so that anything goes. Is freedom doing everything? No. Freedom is respecting the limits of halal and haram, and after that move freely, because everything is permitted to you after that. That is the perception of freedom in Islam and in the Sharia.

And it is very important, very significant to build up these foundations in one another. Next, look at their question. They did not drag it out. They say: "Fa murna" – meaning: "O Messenger of Allah, we have come, we have barely made it here.

The road is unsafe. We have invested effort and toil. We do not have the opportunity to come to you every day. That is why we want to ask you something." And they truly hit the mark; they asked the right question. They say: "So that we may convey it to those who sent us and enter Jannah." Look, my brothers, at what the goal of true people is, of rational, intelligent, wise people. The goal is to enter Jannah.

That is the goal. That is the wish. There are many companions of the Messenger of Allah, sallallahu alayhi wa sallam, who asked: "O Messenger of Allah, dullani 'ala 'amalin yudkhiluniyal-jannah" – O Messenger of Allah, direct me to a deed that will admit me into Jannah. The companions had heard about Jannah. They flew towards Jannah. They hastened towards Jannah. Exactly as Allah, subhanahu wa ta'ala, said: "Hasten
towards the mercy and forgiveness of your Lord and towards Jannah." Compete, race, vie with one another on the way to Jannah.

Flee, run to Allah, subhanahu wa ta'ala, and to Jannah – hasten. They knew that life is limited. Here, their life has passed, and the life of many generations after them has passed. And our, our life too is flowing,

our life is being used up. Wise are those people who hasten to Jannah, who hasten to Jannah. It is said that all the verbs that are used, which speak of moving towards Jannah and towards Allah, do not say "go", but rather "hasten, run, compete".

Well, that is why the companions say: "How can we enter Jannah? Teach us the elementary information and rulings that we will adhere to, and on the basis of which we will enter, enter Jannah." So, that is what they asked first.

And then, after that, they asked him – they asked the Messenger of Allah, sallallahu alayhi wa sallam – secondary questions, less important questions. They asked him about kinds of drink and about the vessels in which they could keep their, their, well, drinks.

So, it is very important for a person to have priorities in life: first you ask about what is most important and first you do what matters most to you, and only then what is less important, what is, well, less important. Then the Prophet, sallallahu alayhi wa sallam – just as this was a team of the best students, he, alayhis-salatu was-salam, was the best teacher – explained to them in one sentence the way to Jannah.

He explained to them the way to Jannah in one sentence, briefly. It says: "Amarahum bil-imani billah" – first he commanded them to believe in Allah. Note, the word "iman" was known among the companions, among the Arabs, but in the Sharia iman means something else,

just as the word "salat", prayer, means one thing in Arabic and another in the Sharia, because the Prophet, sallallahu alayhi wa sallam, defined it in a special way. And then he asks them – see what an educator this is – he says: "A tadruna mal-iman?" – do you know what iman is?
Do you know what iman is? He wants to engage them, to awaken their interest, to awaken their attention.

And they might have known how to answer, but they were not so ill-mannered as to miss the opportunity to hear the best answer from the best teacher, from the Messenger of Allah, Muhammad, sallallahu alayhi wa sallam. They say, with the utmost good manners (adab): "Allahu wa rasuluhu a'lam" –

Allah and His Messenger know best, Allah and His Messenger know best, best. And then the Prophet, sallallahu alayhi wa sallam, explained iman to them, defined iman for them. Iman, by the way, when it is taught in the mekteb (Qur'an school), you ask: what do we say, what is iman, what are the pillars (rukn) of iman?

One says: belief in Allah, in the angels, in the books, in the messengers, in the Last Day and in Allah's decree. Isn't that so? It is. And the Prophet, sallallahu alayhi wa sallam, defines iman like this: that iman is the shahadah, performing the prayer, zakat, fasting, and that it is also part of iman to set aside a fifth of their, their spoils of war, of their war booty, for the Muslim community. What does this indicate? This indicates, my brothers, as the Islamic scholars say,

that deeds… that there is no iman without deeds, without work and without effort, and that those groups and individuals are in great error who wanted to explain to themselves, or in some way to make things easier according to their [unclear], saying that belief and iman is only recognition with the heart, or only testimony with the tongue.

What is needed is firm conviction in the heart, uttering it with the tongue, and then confirming it with deeds: confirming it with prayer, and zakat, and fasting, and Hajj, and struggle in the way of Allah, the result of which is spoils of war, and from the spoils of war one fifth is then given to the Muslim, well, community.

And then, for example, that claim which had become established among our folk and among our people: "I believe with my heart." That is not the complete definition of iman. The complete definition of iman is firm conviction in the heart, then testifying to that truth with the tongue, saying "La ilaha illallah, Muhammadur-Rasulullah", and then validating it.

Validating it, mind you, validating it with prayer, zakat, fasting, Hajj, struggle, effort in the way of Allah, carrying out all of Allah's commands, avoiding all His, well… Here I do not want to comment now on the shahadah, prayer and fasting individually, because we would go very, well, we would go very far afield.
Here it is very important that we also grasp a few more important facts and truths, and that is the importance, the importance of calling to Allah the Exalted.

Mind you, these people did not come only so that they themselves would learn; rather, they said: "We want to learn from you, O Messenger of Allah, and inform the people we have left behind us, behind us."

It is very important, my dear brothers. Islam spreads through da'wah, in the way of Allah, through calling to Allah the Exalted, subhanahu wa ta'ala, and calling to the truth and to the right path. That is not the role only of scholars and hodjas and imams.

That is their greatest role, their greatest obligation, let us be clear, let us understand one another. But all of us must be imams, hodjas and callers (da'i), callers to Allah, jalla sha'nuhu. All of us, every Muslim, every person – every person can do it and every person must do it.

And whenever da'wah and the call to Allah, jalla sha'nuhu, is affirmed and active, and when it exists in a society, evil retreats and is pushed back and marginalised. So, that is the rule: enjoining good and forbidding evil, when it exists, when it lives in a people, in an environment, in a society, then evil is pushed back. It cannot disappear completely, because Allah has allowed it to exist, but it is marginalised, pushed back and insignificant.

But when da'wah disappears, when we give up this principle and this institution which is called enjoining good and forbidding evil – speaking about the truth, promoting it, speaking out wherever we find ourselves – then evil grows stronger, and there is a danger that it will dominate and take over completely.

And that is why it is very important, very significant that we treat our people in the most beautiful way, in the most beautiful way. Our people here, my dear brothers, have gone through a century of hard trials, full of great challenges, great crises. So, five systems and state orders have succeeded one another over this people, here in Sandžak, in Bosnia and in the Balkans in general, and all of them were aimed at erasing our religious identity, and our survival in this form is a phenomenon.

That is rahmatun min Rabbil-'alamin, the mercy of the Lord of all the worlds and an honour from the Lord of all the worlds. The truth is so deeply rooted in us that it simply continues to bear fruit. They squeezed us so much, they dissolved us so much, they did so much to us, all to dilute us, simply to suck that energy out of us – yet the pulse of truth kept beating in us and continues to bear fruit, to give blessing (barakah), to produce such individuals, to produce such congregations, to produce such scholars and imams and, of course, such other workers,

distinguished in various fields and at various, well, at various levels. And that is why we must be gentle and good towards our people, who are basically good, and we should not much… It is not easy to live a whole life without a mekteb, without knowledge, without the Qur'an, without prayer, etc.

These people are in great difficulty. It is not easy even to explain things to them, but we must talk, we must explain, we must call. Because, regardless of the fact that great good (khayr) and a great awakening have happened since the 90s, still a very small percentage of our people –

and a very small percentage of our people – goes to the mosque and fulfils the basic obligations towards the Lord of the heavens. As long as even one member of our congregation [unclear] does not know how to pray and does not pray, then, to Allah, jalla wa 'ala, we must not be at ease and at peace.

And as long as there is one child, one young man or young woman, who is not in circles where they can learn the basic things about their religion, we must not be content and at peace. And if all of us who are in the mosques were to become maximally engaged and maximally active and maximally far-reaching in that sense, we would truly, truly change the situation to…

Next, when the deeds are accepted, a person will enter Jannah. When He accepts the deeds, you will enter Jannah. Because they say: "Give us some deeds to do which will admit us into Jannah," then the Prophet says: these are those deeds.
Which means: if you do them, and Allah accepts them, you will, in sha Allah, enter Jannah. Then the Prophet, sallallahu alayhi wa sallam, forbade them four kinds of vessels.

Four kinds of vessels. Those were vessels they made from gourds – vessels they made, that is, the hollow of gourds – then they would make hollows from palm roots, from other trees and so on, and then they would coat them with some coatings, pitch and the like.
And in those vessels they would put dates, they would put various kinds of fruit and so on. Then the Prophet, sallallahu alayhi wa sallam, forbade them that.
Why had he forbidden them that? Because fruit in such vessels, which were dark, would quickly ferment and simply acquire an intoxicating property, turn into alcohol.

And the Prophet, sallallahu alayhi wa sallam, recommended that they store, store, that is, put things in and use, vessels of leather, of leather. Then one of them stood up and said: "O Messenger of Allah, in the place where we live there are many rats, or mice," and he says, "they will not leave a single one of those vessels, that is, those leather bags, without destroying it," and so on. Then the Prophet said: "Even if the mice eat them, even if the mice eat them, even if the mice eat them." In any case, this kind of vessel was forbidden like this at the beginning. And then the Prophet, sallallahu alayhi wa sallam, abrogated that, in principle,

that ruling too, and he said… he made it easier both for them and for us, and he said to them: "Kullu muskirin haram" – everything that intoxicates, regardless of what vessel it is in: transparent, non-transparent, wooden, non-wooden, glass and so on.

So, do not pay attention to the vessels; rather, pay attention to one main rule, and that is: everything that intoxicates, in small or large quantities, in small or in large quantities. And that is why this is a golden rule,

a universal rule. Today people, for example, call various drinks in various ways – alcoholic drinks that have an intoxicating property – this and that and so on. Don't pay attention to what they call it; just ask whether it has an intoxicating property.

If it has an intoxicating property, then it is haram. If it does not have an intoxicating property, whatever they call it, it is permissible, it is fine. Then, after that, the Prophet, sallallahu alayhi wa sallam, says: "Remember this well and convey it to those to whom you will return."

"Remember this well." It is very important, then, for a person to memorise, to learn by heart, to learn knowledge by heart. By heart – it is very important to exercise the brain, to memorise information and to learn by heart. That is very important, very significant.

And when you learn something, learn it really precisely. If someone asks you something, you know it, so that you can recount it, regardless of what field it was in – so, that you can recount it, that is perfect. And that is why the Prophet, sallallahu alayhi wa sallam, says: "Ihfazuhu wa akhbiru bihi man wara'akum" –

learn this well, understand this well and convey it to those to whom you will, in sha Allahu ta'ala, return. And note, this group of men, this people of theirs, was privileged among other things in that the first Friday prayer (jumu'ah) the Muslims prayed

outside Madinah was in their place – the first jumu'ah outside the Madinah of the Messenger of Allah. These people prayed it. So, as is stated in the hadith in Imam Bukhari: "Inna awwala jumu'atin jummi'at ba'da jumu'atin fi masjidi Rasulillahi, sallallahu alayhi wa sallam, fi masjidi 'Abdil-Qaysi bi Juwatha minal-Bahrayn."

So, in the mosque of this tribe of Rabi'ah, in that region, over there in Al-Ahsa, that is, towards present-day Bahrain. Look what a [unclear], what a privilege it is that this people and this esteemed delegation are mentioned in this way, for this good.

Here, dear brothers, respected sisters, is how the Messenger of Allah, sallallahu alayhi wa sallam, conducted a dialogue, how a dialogue between serious people went, how the companions of the Messenger of Allah, sallallahu alayhi wa sallam, made use of the presence of the Prophet, sallallahu alayhi wa sallam: simply, when they had the opportunity to ask, they asked about what was most beneficial, most important, most essential, and they passed it on to us.

These first generations remembered this, then preserved it and passed it on through authentic chains of narrators to us. Here we are today, far from Madinah and far from the Prophet, sallallahu alayhi wa sallam, in time, but very close in essence, very close in essence. We read what the Prophet, sallallahu alayhi wa sallam, said, and we are convinced that this is how it was, just as we are convinced that we are [unclear].

And now, if someone wanted to verify every hadith of the Prophet, sallallahu alayhi wa sallam – whether the Messenger of Allah, sallallahu alayhi wa sallam, really said it or not – he can verify it, he can verify it. Well, that is what distinguishes this ummah: it has a methodology for verifying both the hadiths and the channels through which the noble Qur'an came.

Because about all those who transmitted the Qur'an and the hadith of the Prophet, sallallahu alayhi wa sallam – everything is written down about them. You could have been any person back then engaged in any job or occupation,

but no one would pay special attention to you. But if you dared to transmit the Qur'an or a hadith of the Messenger of Allah, sallallahu alayhi wa sallam, they knew everything about you, everything about you is written down: what you were like, who you were, your character, and traits, and virtues, trustworthy, untrustworthy, whether he made mistakes or did not make mistakes – everything is known.

And to this very day you can come and read through [unclear] of the Prophet and the channels through which the hadith of the Messenger of Allah, sallallahu alayhi wa sallam, came to us, and truly convince yourself that it is so. May Allah, jalla sha'nuhu, reward you; may Allah, subhanahu wa ta'ala, accept it, receive it.

I ask Allah, jalla wa 'ala, to make us among the true seekers of knowledge, of the most sublime virtues and values, that Allah, subhanahu wa ta'ala, gather us in goodness (khayr) and in good, that He help us to continue following this best generation and to meet them, headed by the Messenger of Allah, to tell them, to tell the Messenger of Allah in Jannah how we struggled here and prevailed, in sha Allahu ta'ala, walking his paths and in his footsteps.
Allah knows best. Thanks be to Allah, subhanahu wa ta'ala, thanks be to Him at the beginning and at the end, and blessings, blessings and peace upon the Prophet Muhammad… [unclear]
